# Model and source

* Citation: Mohamed M-EF, Klunder B, Lacerda AP, Othman AA. Exposure-Response
  Analyses for Upadacitinib Efficacy and Safety in the Crohn's Disease CELEST
  Study and Bridging to the Extended-Release Formulation. *Clin Pharmacol
  Ther*. 2020;107(3):639-649.
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1668> (open access, PMC7027977).
  Parameter estimates are in the Supporting Information: Tables S3 and S4
  (population PK), S5 (Markov models), S6 (endoscopic regressions) and S7
  (NONMEM control streams).

The paper extends the upadacitinib population PK model to patients with
Crohn's disease (CD), characterises the absorption of the extended-release (ER)
tablet from a phase 1 study, and links exposure to six efficacy end points of
the 16-week CELEST induction period. All eight models are packaged:

| Model | What it is | Source |
|-------|------------|--------|
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib` | Two-compartment PK in healthy, RA and CD subjects (IR), with the ER absorption branch | Tables S3, S4 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_hv_er` | The ER formulation study fit in healthy subjects (IR and ER) | Table S4 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_clinresp` | Markov model, clinical response, driven by time-varying concentration | Table S5 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_clinrem` | Markov model, clinical remission 2.8/1.0, driven by steady-state Cmin | Tables S5, S7 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_cdai150` | Markov model, CDAI < 150, driven by steady-state Cmin | Table S5 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_endoimp25` | Emax regression, endoscopic response 25%, driven by Cave | Table S6 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_endoimp` | Emax regression, endoscopic response 50%, driven by Cave | Table S6 |
| `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_endorem` | Emax regression, endoscopic remission, driven by Cave | Table S6 |

```{r load}
mod_pk <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib")
mod_hv <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_hv_er")
mod_resp <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_clinresp")
mod_rem <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_clinrem")
mod_cdai <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_cdai150")
mod_er25 <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_endoimp25")
mod_er50 <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_endoimp")
mod_erem <- readModelDb("Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_endorem")

# Two rxode2 warnings are expected here and carry no information: the
# disease- and phase-gated random effects of the PK model (an eta multiplied by
# a 0/1 indicator) cannot be mu-referenced, and the Markov and regression
# models have no random effects, so a multi-subject solve has no 'omega'.
# Only those two messages are muffled; any other warning still shows.
quiet_known <- function(expr) {
  withCallingHandlers(expr, warning = function(w) {
    if (grepl("non-mu referenced|without 'omega'", conditionMessage(w))) {
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  })
}
solve_quiet <- function(...) quiet_known(rxode2::rxSolve(...))
```

## Structure

**PK.** Two compartments with first-order absorption after a lag time.
Women have 15% lower CL/F and 25% lower Vc/F than men; CL/F scales with
creatinine clearance (exponent 0.313) and Vc/F with body weight (exponent
0.490). RA patients have 22% lower CL/F than healthy subjects and CD patients;
both patient groups absorb 1.63 times faster than healthy subjects. Between-subject
variability on CL/F is 16% in healthy subjects, 27% in RA and 41% in CD.
The ER tablet splits the absorbed dose between a slow first-order route
(44.6%, Ka 0.100 1/h) and a 6.11 h zero-order input into the central
compartment, both after a 0.225 h lag, with 74.2% bioavailability relative to
the IR capsule. In `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib` that ER branch is attached to
the final IR model, which is how the paper simulated ER regimens in CD
(Table 2); `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib_hv_er` is the study fit itself, in which
the IR absorption was re-estimated in healthy subjects. An ER dose is two
dose records: one into `depot` and one into `central` with `rate = -2`.

**Clinical end points.** Each is a three-state continuous-time Markov model
(no response, response, dropout; Figure S3). Upadacitinib multiplies the
no-response to response rate K01 by `1 + Emax * C / (EC50 + C)` (Supplement
Methods Equation 1). A factor fitted to the placebo arm multiplies both K01 and
K10, and K01 is raised early in treatment: by a factor of 4.60 in the first
two weeks for clinical response (Table S5 footnote c); by adding 1.57 (two
weeks, clinical remission) or 3.60 (four weeks, CDAI < 150) to the drug-effect
factor (footnotes d and e). The concentration `C` is the time-varying plasma
concentration for clinical response, and the individual steady-state minimum
concentration for the other two. The state probabilities are ODE states
(`s_noresp`, `s_resp`, `s_dropout`), and the outputs (`prob_clinresp`,
`prob_clinrem`, `prob_cdai150`) count responders who have not dropped out,
the nonresponder-imputation (NRI) proportion of Figure 4.

**Endoscopic end points.** `P = Placebo + (Max - Placebo) * Cave / (EC50 + Cave)`
(Supplement Methods Equation 2), one assessment per patient at week 12 or 16.

# Population

CELEST (NCT02365649) randomised 220 adults with moderately-to-severely active
Crohn's disease (CDAI 220-450, SES-CD >= 6, or >= 4 for ileal-only disease)
and an inadequate response or intolerance to an immunomodulator or anti-TNF
therapy to placebo or immediate-release upadacitinib 3, 6, 12 or 24 mg twice
daily or 24 mg once daily for 16 weeks. The exposure-response analyses used
216 of them: 57% women, 86% White, mean age 40.8 years, mean weight 75.7 kg,
mean baseline CDAI 300 and SES-CD 14.9; 96% had failed at least one TNF
antagonist (Table 1). The population PK analysis pooled 753 subjects from
six studies: healthy volunteers, RA patients from one phase 1 substudy and two
phase 2 studies, and 180 CELEST patients with PK samples (Table S2; the ER
study, a further 71 healthy subjects, was fitted separately).

```{r population}
str(quiet_known(mod_pk())$population)
str(mod_rem()$population)
```

# Virtual cohort

Covariates for a CD cohort are drawn from the CELEST summaries: 57% women
(Table 1), body weight log-normal with mean 75.7 kg and SD 20.1 kg truncated
to the observed 39-152 kg, and creatinine clearance log-normal with mean
111 mL/min and SD 35 mL/min truncated to the observed 43-253 mL/min (Table S2,
CELEST column). One set of 200 virtual patients is given every regimen.

```{r cohort}
# rxode2 draws the random effects from its own per-thread stream, so the cohort
# differs between machines. Every assertion below is a centre or quantile check
# that holds for any cohort the model can produce.
set.seed(20200301)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20200301)
n_per_arm <- 200L

rlnorm_ms <- function(n, m, s, lo, hi) {
  sdlog <- sqrt(log(1 + (s / m)^2))
  pmin(pmax(rlnorm(n, log(m) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog), lo), hi)
}
cohort <- tibble(
  pid = seq_len(n_per_arm),
  SEXF = rbinom(n_per_arm, 1, 0.57),
  WT = rlnorm_ms(n_per_arm, 75.7, 20.1, 39, 152),
  CRCL = rlnorm_ms(n_per_arm, 111.3, 35.1, 43.3, 253.1)
)

regimens <- tribble(
  ~regimen, ~form, ~dose, ~tau,
  "Placebo", "IR", 0, 12,
  "3 mg BID", "IR", 3, 12,
  "6 mg BID", "IR", 6, 12,
  "12 mg BID", "IR", 12, 12,
  "18 mg BID", "IR", 18, 12,
  "24 mg BID", "IR", 24, 12,
  "24 mg QD", "IR", 24, 24,
  "7.5 mg QD ER", "ER", 7.5, 24,
  "15 mg QD ER", "ER", 15, 24,
  "30 mg QD ER", "ER", 30, 24,
  "45 mg QD ER", "ER", 45, 24,
  "60 mg QD ER", "ER", 60, 24
) |>
  mutate(rid = row_number(), FORM_UPA_ER = as.integer(form == "ER"))
summary(cohort[, c("SEXF", "WT", "CRCL")])
```

# Steady-state exposures (Table 2)

## The occasion effect on the lag time

At phase 2 visits the lag time is `0.469 * exp((exp(eta)^8 - 1) / 8)` with
`eta ~ N(0, 0.0936)` (Table S3). The Box-Cox shape of 8 bounds the lag below at
0.469 x exp(-1/8) = 0.41 h but gives it a very long right tail:

```{r lag-tail}
lag_q <- tibble(
  quantile = c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95),
  eta = qnorm(quantile, 0, sqrt(0.0936))
) |>
  mutate(lag_h = 0.469 * exp((exp(eta)^8 - 1) / 8))
knitr::kable(lag_q, digits = 3, caption = "Quantiles of the phase 2 occasion lag time (h).")
p_over_12h <- 1 - pnorm(log(8 * log(12 / 0.469) + 1) / 8, 0, sqrt(0.0936))
p_over_12h
stopifnot(abs(p_over_12h - 0.09) < 0.005)
```

About 9% of occasions draw a lag longer than a twice-daily dosing interval,
which in simulation behaves like a delayed or missed dose; in a few percent of
patients the draw is so large (10^4 h and more) that rxode2 cannot solve the
profile and returns `NA`. The model carries the occasion effect as published.
Table 2, however, summarises the empirical-Bayes profiles of the CELEST
patients, whose occasion effects are shrunk towards zero, so the exposure
summaries below hold the occasion effect at its median (`eta = 0`, a lag of
0.469 h) by replacing one line of the model. Every other random effect is
simulated.

```{r pk-model-sim}
mod_pk_sim <- quiet_known(
  rxode2::rxode2(mod_pk) |>
    rxode2::model(tlag_ir <- exp(ltlag + etaltlag * STUDY_UPA_PHASE1))
)
```

Each virtual patient is dosed for 13 days and observed over the next dosing
interval. The event table still carries the occasion index `OCC` (occasion 1
for the run-in, 2 for the observed interval), which the model requires.

```{r pk-events}
t_ss <- 312 # h, start of the observed dosing interval
make_pk_events <- function(reg) {
  tidyr::crossing(cohort, reg) |>
    mutate(id = (rid - 1L) * n_per_arm + pid) |>
    group_by(id) |>
    group_modify(function(d, key) {
      n_runin <- t_ss / d$tau
      dose <- tibble(
        time = c(0, t_ss), amt = d$dose, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot",
        ii = c(d$tau, 0), addl = c(n_runin - 1L, 0L), rate = 0, OCC = c(1L, 2L)
      )
      if (d$FORM_UPA_ER == 1L) dose <- bind_rows(dose, mutate(dose, cmt = "central", rate = -2))
      obs <- tibble(
        time = t_ss + seq(0, d$tau, by = 0.25), amt = 0, evid = 0L,
        cmt = "central", ii = 0, addl = 0L, rate = 0, OCC = 2L
      )
      bind_rows(dose, obs) |>
        mutate(
          regimen = d$regimen, dose_mg = d$dose, tau = d$tau, SEXF = d$SEXF,
          WT = d$WT, CRCL = d$CRCL, FORM_UPA_ER = d$FORM_UPA_ER, DIS_RA = 0L,
          DIS_CD = 1L, STUDY_UPA_PHASE1 = 0L
        )
    }) |>
    ungroup() |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}
ev_pk <- make_pk_events(filter(regimens, dose > 0))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(ev_pk[ev_pk$evid == 0, c("id", "time")]))
sim_pk <- solve_quiet(mod_pk_sim, ev_pk,
  keep = c("regimen", "dose_mg", "tau", "FORM_UPA_ER"),
  returnType = "data.frame"
)
stopifnot(!anyNA(sim_pk$Cc))
```

```{r figure-ss, fig.height = 5}
sim_pk |>
  mutate(tad = time - t_ss) |>
  group_by(regimen, tad) |>
  summarise(q05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05), q50 = median(Cc), q95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(regimen = factor(regimen, levels = regimens$regimen)) |>
  ggplot(aes(tad, q50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~regimen, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "Upadacitinib (ng/mL)",
    caption = "Median and 5th-95th percentiles over one steady-state dosing interval, virtual CD cohort."
  )
```

## PKNCA

Cmax, Cmin and Cave over the observed interval, per patient and regimen.

```{r pknca}
conc_df <- sim_pk |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, regimen)
dose_df <- ev_pk |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1, cmt == "depot", time == t_ss) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, regimen)
intervals <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(start = t_ss, end = t_ss + 12, regimen = regimens$regimen[regimens$tau == 12 & regimens$dose > 0]),
  data.frame(start = t_ss, end = t_ss + 24, regimen = regimens$regimen[regimens$tau == 24])
) |>
  mutate(cmax = TRUE, cmin = TRUE, cav = TRUE)
nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_df, Cc ~ time | regimen + id),
  PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | regimen + id),
  intervals = intervals
))
nca_df <- as.data.frame(nca)
stopifnot(!anyNA(nca_df$PPORRES))
```

Table 2 gives the median (5th-95th percentile) exposures. For the IR regimens
they come from the empirical-Bayes estimates of the CELEST patients, for the
ER regimens from simulation.

```{r nca-compare}
table2 <- tribble(
  ~regimen, ~cav, ~cmax, ~cmin,
  "3 mg BID", 6.9, 21.8, 1.2,
  "6 mg BID", 14.9, 40.2, 2.6,
  "12 mg BID", 26.7, 80.7, 4.9,
  "24 mg BID", 55.1, 176, 7.8,
  "24 mg QD", 25.1, 161, 1.7,
  "7.5 mg QD ER", 6.4, 17.3, 1.4,
  "15 mg QD ER", 12.9, 34.7, 2.9,
  "30 mg QD ER", 25.8, 69.3, 5.7,
  "45 mg QD ER", 38.7, 104.0, 8.6,
  "60 mg QD ER", 51.6, 138.6, 11.4
)
cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = filter(nca_df, regimen %in% table2$regimen),
  reference = table2,
  by = "regimen",
  units = c(cav = "ng/mL", cmax = "ng/mL", cmin = "ng/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = "Simulated median vs Mohamed 2020 Table 2. * differs by more than 20%.")
```

```{r nca-gate}
med <- nca_df |>
  group_by(regimen, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(sim = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(pivot_longer(table2, -regimen, names_to = "PPTESTCD", values_to = "pub"),
    by = c("regimen", "PPTESTCD")
  ) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (sim / pub - 1))
knitr::kable(
  med |> group_by(PPTESTCD) |>
    summarise(median_pct = median(pct), max_abs_pct = max(abs(pct))),
  digits = 1, caption = "Percent difference from Table 2 by metric, across regimens."
)
# Cave depends only on CL/F and the relative bioavailability; a wrong
# clearance, sex or creatinine-clearance effect, bioavailability or unit moves
# every regimen together by tens of percent.
stopifnot(
  abs(median(med$pct[med$PPTESTCD == "cav"])) < 10,
  abs(median(med$pct[med$PPTESTCD == "cmax"])) < 15,
  abs(median(med$pct[med$PPTESTCD == "cmin"])) < 25
)
```

Cave, which depends only on CL/F and the relative bioavailability, lands within
about 10% of Table 2 for every regimen, IR and ER. Cmax and Cmin of the IR
regimens agree to a similar degree, although Table 2 summarises the 180 CELEST
patients' own empirical-Bayes profiles rather than a simulated cohort.

The ER rows agree less well in this population simulation: Cmax medians run
roughly 10-17% low and Cmin medians scatter widely between regimens. The ER
absorption parameters carry very large variability (Ka 111%, zero-order
duration 121%, logit first-order fraction variance 1.49; Table S4), so the
median Cmin of 200 patients is unstable, and with that variability the
population profiles are flatter than the typical one. Table S4 also reports
only the variances of a 5 x 5 block of ER random effects, so the packaged
models simulate them as independent, which the paper's simulations did not.
The typical patient, which carries none of that variability, reproduces the
ER rows closely. The check below uses a typical woman (the majority sex in
CELEST) with the CELEST mean creatinine clearance and body weight:

```{r er-typical}
ev_typ_er <- filter(regimens, form == "ER") |>
  mutate(id = row_number()) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    dose <- tibble(
      time = 0, amt = d$dose, evid = 1L, cmt = c("depot", "central"),
      ii = 24, addl = 13L, rate = c(0, -2), OCC = 1L
    )
    obs <- tibble(time = t_ss + seq(0, 24, by = 0.05), amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", ii = 0, addl = 0L, rate = 0, OCC = 2L)
    bind_rows(dose, obs) |> mutate(regimen = d$regimen)
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(SEXF = 1, WT = 75.7, CRCL = 111.3, FORM_UPA_ER = 1L, DIS_RA = 0L, DIS_CD = 1L, STUDY_UPA_PHASE1 = 0L) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
typ_er <- solve_quiet(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_pk), ev_typ_er, keep = "regimen", returnType = "data.frame") |>
  group_by(regimen) |>
  summarise(cmax = max(Cc), cmin = min(Cc), cav = mean(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(table2, by = "regimen", suffix = c("_typ", "_pub")) |>
  mutate(
    pct_cmax = 100 * (cmax_typ / cmax_pub - 1),
    pct_cmin = 100 * (cmin_typ / cmin_pub - 1),
    pct_cav = 100 * (cav_typ / cav_pub - 1)
  )
knitr::kable(
  select(typ_er, regimen, cmax_typ, cmax_pub, cmin_typ, cmin_pub, cav_typ, cav_pub),
  digits = 2, caption = "Typical CD woman vs Table 2 ER medians (ng/mL)."
)
# Typical-value solve, no random draws: the remaining difference is between a
# typical patient and the median of the paper's simulated cohort.
stopifnot(
  all(abs(typ_er$pct_cmax) < 10),
  all(abs(typ_er$pct_cmin) < 15),
  all(abs(typ_er$pct_cav) < 10)
)
```

## Relative bioavailability of the ER tablet

In the healthy-volunteer formulation fit, the dose-normalised AUC of the ER
tablet relative to the IR capsule must equal the 74.2% relative bioavailability,
because clearance is common to both. Typical values, single doses of 30 mg ER
and 24 mg IR, observed for 10 days.

```{r rel-ba}
hv_typ <- tibble(id = 1:2, FORM_UPA_ER = c(0L, 1L), dose = c(24, 30), SEXF = 0, WT = 74, CRCL = 106.9)
ev_hv <- hv_typ |>
  group_by(id) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    dose <- tibble(time = 0, amt = d$dose, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", rate = 0)
    if (d$FORM_UPA_ER == 1L) dose <- bind_rows(dose, mutate(dose, cmt = "central", rate = -2))
    obs <- tibble(time = c(seq(0, 24, by = 0.1), seq(25, 240, by = 1)), amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", rate = 0)
    bind_rows(dose, obs) |> mutate(FORM_UPA_ER = d$FORM_UPA_ER, SEXF = d$SEXF, WT = d$WT, CRCL = d$CRCL, dose_mg = d$dose)
  }) |>
  ungroup()
sim_hv <- solve_quiet(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_hv), ev_hv, keep = "dose_mg", returnType = "data.frame")
nca_hv <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(dplyr::filter(sim_hv, !is.na(Cc)), Cc ~ time | id),
  PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dplyr::filter(ev_hv, evid == 1, cmt == "depot"), amt ~ time | id),
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 240, auclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE)
)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(id, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  left_join(hv_typ, by = "id") |>
  mutate(auc_per_mg = auclast / dose)
knitr::kable(nca_hv, digits = 3, caption = "Typical healthy male, single dose.")
frel_obs <- nca_hv$auc_per_mg[2] / nca_hv$auc_per_mg[1]
frel_obs
# Same parameters on both sides: the only error is the 240 h truncation and
# the trapezoid.
stopifnot(abs(frel_obs / 0.742 - 1) < 0.02)
```

The ER profile peaks around the end of the 6.1 h zero-order input, and the
slow first-order route keeps its terminal phase flat; this matches the
qualitative shape of Figure S1.

# Markov models: checks that need no cohort

## Probability is conserved

```{r mass-balance}
obs_h <- c(0, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16) * 168
typ <- tibble(id = 1L, SEXF = 1, WT = 75, CRCL = 111, FORM_UPA_ER = 0L)
ev_typ <- bind_rows(
  tibble(id = 1L, time = 0, amt = 12, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", ii = 12, addl = 16 * 14 - 1L),
  tibble(id = 1L, time = obs_h, amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "s_resp", ii = 0, addl = 0L)
) |>
  left_join(typ, by = "id") |>
  arrange(time, desc(evid))
mb <- solve_quiet(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_resp), ev_typ, returnType = "data.frame") |>
  mutate(total = s_noresp + s_resp + s_dropout)
stopifnot(max(abs(mb$total - 1)) < 1e-6)
range(mb$total)
```

## Closed form for the steady-state-Cmin models

With a constant `CTROUGH`, the remission and CDAI < 150 chains are
time-homogeneous within the early window and after it, so the state
probabilities are a product of two matrix exponentials. Both sides use the
same rates, so the bound is tight.

```{r closed-form}
markov_q <- function(k01, k10, k0d, k1d) {
  q <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
  q[1, 2] <- k01
  q[1, 3] <- k0d
  q[2, 1] <- k10
  q[2, 3] <- k1d
  diag(q) <- -rowSums(q)
  q
}
expm_eigen <- function(a) {
  e <- eigen(a)
  Re(e$vectors %*% diag(exp(e$values)) %*% solve(e$vectors))
}
closed_form <- function(p, cmin, t) {
  eff <- 1 + p$emax * (cmin + 0.001) / (p$ec50 + 0.001 + cmin + 0.001)
  early_q <- markov_q(p$k01 * (eff + p$early) * p$s, p$k10 * p$s, p$k0d, p$k1d)
  late_q <- markov_q(p$k01 * eff * p$s, p$k10 * p$s, p$k0d, p$k1d)
  sapply(t, function(tt) {
    pr <- c(1, 0, 0) %*% expm_eigen(early_q * min(tt, p$t_early))
    if (tt > p$t_early) pr <- pr %*% expm_eigen(late_q * (tt - p$t_early))
    pr[2]
  })
}
par_rem <- list(k01 = 0.0000603, k10 = 0.000324, k0d = 0.0000813, k1d = 0.0000158,
  emax = 4.57, ec50 = 6.11, early = 1.57, s = 1.80, t_early = 336)
par_cdai <- list(k01 = 0.0000813, k10 = 0.000309, k0d = 0.0000708, k1d = 0.0000427,
  emax = 4.31, ec50 = 10.2, early = 3.60, s = 1.25, t_early = 672)
grid_h <- sort(c(seq(0, 16 * 168, by = 84), 336, 672))
ev_cf <- tidyr::crossing(id = 1:3, time = grid_h) |>
  mutate(CTROUGH = c(0, 2, 8)[id], amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "s_resp")
cf <- bind_rows(
  solve_quiet(mod_rem, ev_cf, returnType = "data.frame") |>
    mutate(model = "clinrem", prob = prob_clinrem),
  solve_quiet(mod_cdai, ev_cf, returnType = "data.frame") |>
    mutate(model = "cdai150", prob = prob_cdai150)
) |>
  select(model, id, time, prob) |>
  left_join(distinct(ev_cf, id, CTROUGH), by = "id") |>
  group_by(model, CTROUGH) |>
  mutate(closed = closed_form(if (model[1] == "clinrem") par_rem else par_cdai, CTROUGH[1], time)) |>
  ungroup()
max(abs(cf$prob - cf$closed))
stopifnot(max(abs(cf$prob - cf$closed)) < 1e-5)
```

# Efficacy by regimen (Figure 4)

The paper simulated 100 trials of 220 patients per regimen and printed the
median percentage of responders (NRI) at week 12 for the clinical end points
and at week 12/16 for the endoscopic ones (Figure 4). Here each virtual patient
receives every regimen. The two steady-state exposure metrics come from the PK
solve above, with Cave computed by the paper's formula (Table 2 footnote a:
dose x relative bioavailability / (CL/F x tau)) and Cmin the minimum over the
observed interval. The clinical response model carries its own PK and is solved
with 12 weeks of dosing.

```{r er-exposures}
indiv <- sim_pk |>
  group_by(id, regimen) |>
  summarise(cl = first(cl), frel = first(frel), dose_mg = first(dose_mg), tau = first(tau), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(CAV = 1000 * dose_mg * frel / (cl * tau)) |>
  left_join(
    nca_df |> filter(PPTESTCD == "cmin") |> select(id, regimen, CTROUGH = PPORRES),
    by = c("id", "regimen")
  )
pbo <- tibble(id = 0L - seq_len(n_per_arm), regimen = "Placebo", CAV = 0, CTROUGH = 0)
indiv <- bind_rows(select(indiv, id, regimen, CAV, CTROUGH), pbo) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())
stopifnot(!anyNA(indiv$CAV), !anyNA(indiv$CTROUGH))
```

```{r er-static}
wk12 <- 12 * 168
ev_static <- indiv |> mutate(time = wk12, amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "s_resp")
solve_prob <- function(mod, col, ev) {
  solve_quiet(mod, ev, keep = "regimen", returnType = "data.frame") |>
    group_by(regimen) |>
    summarise(pct = 100 * mean(.data[[col]]), .groups = "drop")
}
ev_endo <- select(ev_static, id, regimen, CAV) |> mutate(time = 0, amt = 0, evid = 0L)
res_static <- bind_rows(
  solve_prob(mod_rem, "prob_clinrem", ev_static) |> mutate(endpoint = "Clinical remission 2.8/1.0"),
  solve_prob(mod_cdai, "prob_cdai150", ev_static) |> mutate(endpoint = "CDAI < 150"),
  solve_prob(mod_er25, "prob_endoimp25", ev_endo) |> mutate(endpoint = "Endoscopic response 25%"),
  solve_prob(mod_er50, "prob_endoimp", ev_endo) |> mutate(endpoint = "Endoscopic response 50%"),
  solve_prob(mod_erem, "prob_endorem", ev_endo) |> mutate(endpoint = "Endoscopic remission")
)
```

```{r er-clinresp}
ev_resp <- tidyr::crossing(cohort, regimens) |>
  mutate(id = (rid - 1L) * n_per_arm + pid) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    dose <- tibble(
      time = 0, amt = d$dose, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", ii = d$tau,
      addl = as.integer(16 * 168 / d$tau) - 1L, rate = 0
    )
    if (d$FORM_UPA_ER == 1L) dose <- bind_rows(dose, mutate(dose, cmt = "central", rate = -2))
    obs <- tibble(time = obs_h, amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "s_resp", ii = 0, addl = 0L, rate = 0)
    bind_rows(dose, obs) |>
      mutate(regimen = d$regimen, SEXF = d$SEXF, WT = d$WT, CRCL = d$CRCL, FORM_UPA_ER = d$FORM_UPA_ER)
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
sim_resp <- solve_quiet(mod_resp, ev_resp, keep = "regimen", returnType = "data.frame")
stopifnot(!anyNA(sim_resp$prob_clinresp))
res_resp <- sim_resp |>
  filter(time == wk12) |>
  group_by(regimen) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(prob_clinresp), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(endpoint = "Clinical response")
```

```{r figure-4}
fig4 <- tribble(
  ~regimen, ~`Clinical response`, ~`Clinical remission 2.8/1.0`, ~`CDAI < 150`,
  ~`Endoscopic response 25%`, ~`Endoscopic response 50%`, ~`Endoscopic remission`,
```

Replicates Figure 4 of Mohamed 2020.

```{r figure-4-table}
  arrange(endpoint, regimen) |>
  select(endpoint, regimen, published, pct, diff) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "End point" = endpoint, "Regimen" = regimen, "Figure 4 (%)" = published,
```

```{r figure-4-gate}
er_gate <- er_cmp |>
  group_by(endpoint) |>
  summarise(median_diff = median(diff), q90_abs = quantile(abs(diff), 0.9))
knitr::kable(er_gate, digits = 1)
# A mis-transcribed rate, Emax, EC50 or early-window term shifts a whole panel
# by several points; the published bars are medians of 100 simulated trials
# read to the nearest percentage point.
stopifnot(
  all(abs(er_gate$median_diff) < 3),
  all(er_gate$q90_abs < 5)

```

All six end points reproduce the printed bars of Figure 4 to within about
3 percentage points for every IR and ER regimen, including the placebo arms,
which depend only on the transition rates and the early-window terms. The
clinical-response bars of the ER regimens run 2-3 points above Figure 4, the
largest differences in the figure.

## Clinical response over time (Figure 3)

```{r figure-3}
fig3_regs <- c("Placebo", "3 mg BID", "6 mg BID", "12 mg BID", "24 mg BID", "24 mg QD")
sim_resp |>
  filter(regimen %in% fig3_regs) |>
  group_by(regimen, time) |>
  summarise(
    nri = 100 * mean(prob_clinresp),
    on_study = 100 * mean(prob_clinresp / (1 - s_dropout)), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(nri, on_study), names_to = "denominator", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(regimen = factor(regimen, levels = fig3_regs), week = time / 168) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, pct, linetype = denominator)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~regimen) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (weeks)", y = "Clinical response (%)",
    caption = paste(
      "Expected percentage of responders, all randomised (NRI) and among those on study.",
      "Compare with the model lines of Figure 3 of Mohamed 2020."
    )
  )
```

The steep rise over the first two weeks is the early K01 boost; drug arms rise
faster than placebo already in that window, which is why the boost is read as
multiplying the whole drug-modified K01 (Table S5 footnote c) rather than the
placebo rate alone. Figure 3 plots responders among patients still on study,
which sits a few points above the NRI curve that Figure 4 uses.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **ER branch attached to the CD model.** The ER absorption parameters were
  estimated in healthy subjects with all disposition parameters fixed
  (Table S4). The paper's ER simulations in CD combined them with the final IR
  model (Methods; Table 2), and `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib` and
  `_clinresp` do the same. The control stream's ER branch replaces Ka
  outright, so the patient Ka ratio of 1.63 does not apply to the ER tablet.
  The re-estimated IR absorption of the formulation study (Ka 9.68 1/h,
  lag 0.247 h) and its residual error are kept only in `_hv_er`.
* **ER random effects are diagonal.** The formulation study estimated the five
  ER random effects as a 5 x 5 block (`$OMEGA BLOCK(5)`, Table S7), but only
  the variances are reported (Table S4), so the packaged models omit the
  covariances. Population medians of ER Cmax and Cmin therefore differ from
  the paper's simulated Table 2 rows by more than those of a typical patient
  do (see "Steady-state exposures").
* **Lag-time inter-occasion variability.** Table S3 reports a Box-Cox shape of
  8 for the inter-occasion variability on the lag time at phase 2 visits. With
  that shape the occasion lag time is bounded below (0.41 h) but has a very
  long right tail: roughly 9% of occasions draw a lag above 12 h, which in
  simulation acts like a delayed or missed dose, and the most extreme draws
  make rxode2 return `NA` for that patient. This is encoded as published; the
  population exposure summaries in this vignette hold the occasion effect at
  its median instead (see "The occasion effect on the lag time"). Event tables for
  `Mohamed_2020_upadacitinib` need an `OCC` column, and rxode2 draws a separate
  occasion effect per patient only when patients have at least two `OCC`
  levels. Phase 1 subjects carry the interindividual lag eta instead
  (`STUDY_UPA_PHASE1 = 1`). The checker reports `OCC` as a covariate not used in
  `model()`, because it is consumed by the `| OCC` nesting in `ini()`.
* **Clinical response PK.** `_clinresp` carries the CD arm of the PK model at
  the typical lag time, without the occasion effect, and with the PK parameters
  fixed: the Markov fit took each patient's empirical-Bayes PK as given.
* **Creatinine-clearance reference.** The control streams divide by
  106.9 mL/min; Tables S3 and S4 print 107. The packaged models use 106.9.
* **Early-window boundary and the minc guard.** Table S7 prints the control
  stream of the clinical remission model only. Its form (K01 raised while
  `T <= 336` h, Hill coefficient fixed to 1, and 0.001 ng/mL added to the
  concentration and the EC50) is assumed for the other two Markov models, with
  the four-week window of CDAI < 150 taken as `t <= 672` h. Time 0 is the
  first dose.
* **Markov K01 and K10 values.** The control stream fixes the remission K01 and
  K10 at 10^-4.2216 and 10^-3.4855 per hour (6.00e-5 and 3.27e-4), whereas
  Table S5 prints 0.0000603 and 0.000324. The differences are below 1%; the
  packaged models use Table S5.
* **State occupancy instead of transition probabilities.** The control stream
  integrates transition probabilities from each patient's previous observed
  state, which is what the likelihood needs. For simulation the packaged
  models integrate the population state probabilities from everyone starting
  in the no-response state, which is true at baseline for all three end points
  in CELEST (CDAI >= 220 at entry; remission assessed among patients with
  stool frequency >= 4.0 or abdominal pain >= 2.0; response is relative to
  baseline).
* **Exposure covariates.** `CTROUGH` (Cmin) and `CAV` (Cave) are constant per
  patient from the first dose, as in the source data set, and are 0 for
  placebo. Here they are computed from simulated steady-state profiles of the
  PK model; the paper used each CELEST patient's empirical-Bayes PK.
* **Placeholder residual errors.** The Markov and regression likelihoods are
  categorical (Bernoulli), so the source has no residual error. Each model
  carries a fixed additive SD of 0.001 on its probability output so that
  nlmixr2 accepts it; it is not from the source.
* **Virtual cohort.** Creatinine clearance and body weight are drawn
  independently from log-normal distributions matching the CELEST means and
  SDs; sex is drawn at the Table 1 proportion. The covariates of the real
  cohort are correlated, which the virtual cohort does not reproduce.
* **Safety.** The paper found no exposure-response trend for haemoglobin
  decrease, lymphopenia, herpes zoster, pneumonia or serious infections and
  fitted no model to them (Figure 5), so there is nothing to package.
